tagline.text: A seven-tier waterfall in a mountain gorge in Tibiao, with rope-assisted trekking

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: June–February (when water is plentiful; avoid right after heavy rain)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half day (3–4 hours including the round-trip trek)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–700 (per person, covering local transport, fees and guide)

children.text: Bugtong Bato Falls is a seven-tier waterfall in a mountain gorge in Tibiao, Antique, in northwestern Panay. Most visitors climb with a guide to the lower three tiers and swim in the pools, then come back down to try the town's signature kawa bath.

Bugtong Bato Falls lies deep in the hills of Barangay Tuno in the municipality of Tibiao in Antique, northwestern Panay. Tibiao is a town where the mountain range rises just a short way inland from the coastal highway, and it calls itself the "Eco-Adventure Capital of Panay Island." This waterfall is its best-known attraction. The falls run in seven tiers, and the name is said to come from the way the falls hang in the middle of a lone rock. The origin of the name is explained a little differently from source to source, so it is not certain.
What visitors actually go to see are the lower three tiers. The section up to the third tier is described as reaching a height of up to about

(150 ft), and each tier has a pool at its base where you can swim. Tier four and above is not reached by the same trail. It requires a long climb up a different mountain route that, according to local information, is a separate trek of about
4 hours
more. A typical visit therefore consists of walking from the starting point to the first falls in about
30 minutes
, then climbing with ropes to the second and third tiers.

The trail is a country path that follows the gorge, crossing streams and forest, and passing small rice terraces and cows grazing along the way. You cross two bamboo suspension bridges, and in places you can still see trees that Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) knocked down in 2013. The water from the falls flows into the Tibiao River, where you can go kayaking and tubing downstream. After the trek, the classic local routine is to return to the village and wash off the sweat in a kawa bath, soaking in a large iron cauldron.
This is less a trip for the falls alone and more a good fit for a day or two of country life near Boracay. It is about
2 hours

by road from Caticlan, so you can set aside one day from a Boracay trip. Public transport connections are inconvenient and facilities are few, so we recommend leaving early, seeing the falls around midday and finishing with a kawa bath in the afternoon. This guide compares the fares and travel times from blogs and travel notes posted between 2011 and 2022. Entrance fees, guide fees and motorcycle fares change from year to year and differ by source, so ask the Tibiao tourism office or your lodging for current rates before you go.

blocks.title: Seven tiers and swimming in the lower three

children.text: Each of tiers one to three has a pool at its base that is good for swimming. The first tier is the most visited, with easy access and a wide pool. The third tier is the smallest but has deep blue water and is the deepest; one guide gives its depth as about
. That figure is unconfirmed, so ask your guide about the depth before you jump in.

blocks.title: Rope climbs to tiers two and three

children.text: From the first tier to the second you climb a short, steep section with steps and a nylon rope. The third tier means swimming across the second pool and then pulling yourself up a wet rock face on a rope, which is slippery and difficult. Only some visitors go this far, and if it feels like too much you can still enjoy the lower tiers.

The walk itself is part of the attraction. Streams, forest, small rice terraces and bamboo suspension bridges follow one another, and you may meet cows grazing by the path. The trail is rocky and rough, more a short hike than a gentle stroll.

blocks.title: A course with a village guide

children.text: A guide is mandatory. You register at the barangay desk in Tuno and are assigned a guide, and one guide says a group of five needs two guides. Besides showing the way, the guide points out footholds on the rope sections and keeps an eye on safety at the pools.
A spring near the falls is said to be used for drinking water. Hygiene cannot be guaranteed, so bring your own drinking water and follow your guide's advice if you want to drink local water.
After coming down from the falls, try Tibiao's signature "kawa" bath. A large iron cauldron that was originally used to boil down sugarcane juice is heated over a wood fire for about
30 minutes

and used as an outdoor tub for one or two people. The standard is the herbal kawa with medicinal leaves and flowers, and blogs from 2017–2024 report about ₱200–300 per 30 minutes depending on the resort, with herbal kawa starting at
(salt kawa about ₱299 at Calawag Mountain Resort in 2024). Rates differ by resort, so confirm locally.
You can also go kayaking and tubing on the same Tibiao River. According to one 2022 guide, basic kayaking is

items.title: Half-day waterfall route
items.subtitle: Early start, falls before lunch, kawa in the afternoon

children.text: From Caticlan port in Boracay or from Kalibo, take a bus toward Iloilo or Culasi and get off at Importante Junction in Tibiao. From Caticlan it usually takes about
2 hours
Take a motorcycle (habal-habal) from the junction to the inner part of the village where the kayak and kawa lodgings are, leave your bags and pack snacks and water.
Register at the Barangay Tuno desk, pay the entrance fee and guide fee, and start trekking with your guide.
After crossing streams, rice terraces and bamboo suspension bridges, you reach the first falls in about
30–40 minutes
and swim and rest there.
If you feel up to it, climb the rope sections to the second and third tiers. If it is too hard, take photos at the first tier and head back down.
Back in the village, have lunch. Lodging kitchens can be slow, so it is better to order before you set out for the falls.
Enjoy a kawa bath or river tubing and head back by bus before dark.
If the day feels rushed, we recommend staying one night in Tibiao village. Check the return bus times locally in advance.
Arrive, drop your bags at your lodging and trek to the falls.
Have a kawa bath and dinner at a riverside lodging.
Go kayaking or tubing and check out.
Head toward Culasi and visit neighboring sights such as Mararison Island.
Domestic flights run from Manila Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Caticlan (MPH) or Kalibo (KLO). The flight takes about
1 hour
, but airlines and schedules change by season, so check when you book.
You can also fly to Iloilo (ILO) and travel north, but the road to Tibiao is long, so most people use Caticlan or Kalibo.

items.title: From the junction to the starting point

children.text: From Importante Junction it is about
15 minutes
by motorcycle (habal-habal) to your lodging or the registration desk, reported at around
per person one way. Some drivers may try to steer you to a rival kawa operator, so state clearly where you want to go.
The mountain road is steep and tricycles cannot climb it, so motorcycles are effectively the standard.

A waterfall is only worth seeing with water. Blogs generally say the flow thins in the late dry season (March–May), so they recommend coming after the rains begin, from June or July. Guides also say July to February suits kayaking and tubing.

On the other hand, in the rainy season the gorge can swell suddenly right after heavy rain, and the trail and rocks become very slippery. If it has rained a lot since the day before, ask your guide or lodging about the water level and postpone if they say it is risky. During typhoon season you should also check weather warnings.

Lodging near the falls centers on small places along the Tibiao River. The riverside cottage-style Kayak Inn is reported at around
per person with breakfast extra. Higher up the slope there is also Calawag Mountain Resort, with cottages and a treehouse. Rates and booking methods change from season to season, so confirm locally.

Meals are taken at your lodging or at village eateries. There are no shops on the way to the falls, so bring snacks and water. If you ask a riverside lodging in advance, they may also prepare a boodle fight, a shared meal laid out on banana leaves for a group.
A guide is mandatory. Register at the desk and get a guide assigned.
Sandals or water shoes with firm, non-slip soles are best. Flip-flops are dangerous on the rope sections.
Wear swimwear and put a dry change of clothes and a towel in a waterproof bag.
Keep your phone and wallet in a waterproof pouch, and empty your pockets and belt bag before swimming. One travel account tells of a phone lost by going into the water with a belt bag on.
Bring at least one liter of water. Even a short trek is humid and hot.
Carry cash in small bills. Registration, motorcycles and kawa are generally cash only.
Do the kawa bath after the falls, not before. It washes off sweat and dirt and loosens your muscles.
Going early helps you avoid the midday heat.
During and right after heavy rain, the water in the gorge rises suddenly and the rocks are very slippery. If your guide says it is dangerous, do not climb.
The rope sections at tiers two and three are slippery, and a fall can cause serious injury. If you are out of shape, or are a child or an older person, stop at the first tier.
Pool depth varies by season. Do not dive anywhere you have not checked.
Tier four and above is a separate long trek and not meant for ordinary visitors. Do not go up without a guide.
Fees and rules (entrance fee, how guides are assigned, which sections are open) can change, so check the latest announcements.
When riding a motorcycle taxi, watch the speed and the wet mountain road after rain, and state your destination clearly first.
